In [[number theory]], the '''Shimura correspondence''' is a correspondence between [[modular form]]s ''F'' of half integral weight ''k''+1/2, and modular forms ''f'' of even weight 2''k'', discovered by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Goro Shimura|first=Goro|last=Shimura|year=1973}}. It has the property that the eigenvalue of a [[Hecke operator]] ''T''<sub>''n''<sup>2</sup></sub> on ''F'' is equal to the eigenvalue of ''T''<sub>''n''</sub> on ''f''.

Let <math>f</math> be a holomorphic cusp form with weight <math>(2k+1)/2</math> and character <math>\chi</math> . For any prime number ''p'', let

:<math>\sum^\infty_{n=1}\Lambda(n)n^{-s}=\prod_p(1-\omega_pp^{-s}+(\chi_p)^2p^{2k-1-2s})^{-1}\ ,</math>

where  <math>\omega_p</math>'s are the eigenvalues of the [[Hecke operator]]s <math>T(p^2)</math> determined by ''p''.

Using the [[functional equation (L-function)|functional equation]] of [[L-function]], [[Goro Shimura|Shimura]] showed that

:<math>F(z)=\sum^\infty_{n=1} \Lambda(n)q^n</math>

is a holomorphic [[modular function]] with weight ''2k'' and character <math>\chi^2</math> .

Shimura's proof uses the [[Rankin–Selberg_method#History|Rankin-Selberg convolution]] of <math>f(z)</math> with the theta series <math>\theta_\psi(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^\infty \psi(n) n^\nu e^{2i \pi n^2 z} \ ({\scriptstyle\nu = \frac{1-\psi(-1)}{2}})</math> for various Dirichlet characters <math>\psi</math> then applies [[Weil's converse theorem]].
